patch.value: Self-reported token accounting: any command can report the token cost of its own output so budget spend is attributable at runtime and in CI

Token cost is currently measured externally, in a CI corpus gate, against a fixed sample of commands. That answers whether a release regressed on the sampled corpus; it cannot answer where a specific agent's context budget actually went during a real session, which is the question that matters when an agent runs out of context mid-task. Add an opt-in accounting mode in which a command reports the token cost of the output it just produced, decomposed by section — result rows, envelope, diagnostics, hints — using the same tokenizer as the budget contract so the numbers are comparable to the declared ceilings. This makes budget spend attributable at the granularity of a single invocation and lets an agent adapt: if a read cost far more than expected, it can narrow the next one. It also gives the transcript-replay gate real per-command attribution instead of a session total, turning a regression signal into a diagnosis. Accounting must never itself be expensive or on by default: it is opt-in, adds no cost when off, and its own overhead is measured and asserted.

An opt-in accounting mode reports output token cost decomposed by section, using the same tokenizer as the declared budget contract so the figures are directly comparable; Accounting is off by default and adds no measurable cost when off, asserted by a benchmark; The reported figure is asserted equal to an independent count of the emitted bytes, so the accounting cannot drift from reality; Accounting output is itself bounded and excluded from the accounted total, with the exclusion documented; The transcript-replay regression gate consumes per-command accounting so a session regression identifies the responsible commands; Accounting works identically for CLI and MCP transports, since MCP callers pay the same budget
Every token an agent spends is attributable to the command and section that produced it
Optimizing token cost without per-invocation attribution is guesswork; this converts the whole token-efficiency program from sampling to measurement
Adds an opt-in reporting path to the output pipeline; must be provably zero-cost when disabled
A context overrun becomes a diagnosable event with a named cause instead of an unexplained failure

message: File per-invocation token accounting so budget spend becomes attributable rather than sampled
